title: The Effect of Liquid Housing Wealth on College Enrollment
research_question: Does variation in family housing wealth affect the likelihood that children enroll in college, and if so, are these effects concentrated among lower-resource families? More broadly, how important are total family financial resources—beyond income—in shaping postsecondary investment decisions?
data_description: The primary microdata come from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), used to construct repeated cross-sections of 18–19-year-olds in the survey years 2001, 2003, and 2005 (about 499 observations per year, totaling 1,497), with extensions back to 1980 for cross-decade comparisons. Key variables include college enrollment (defined as completing more than 12 years of schooling within two years), self-reported home value and home equity, mortgage payments and remaining principal, total family income, homeownership status, and detailed household head and respondent demographics. These are merged with state-level unemployment rates (BLS), real per capita income (BEA), college-age population (Census), MSA- and state-level Federal Housing Finance Agency Housing Price Index (HPI) values, and aggregate enrollment counts from IPEDS and the October CPS. The unit of observation is the college-age individual within a household.
institutional_context: The setting is the U.S. housing boom of the late 1990s through 2006, during which real median home prices rose roughly 55% between 1990 and 2005 and extracted home equity as a share of personal income increased more than sixfold. Technological innovations in mortgage origination, falling transaction costs, and the proliferation of home equity loans, home equity lines of credit, and cash-out refinances dramatically increased the liquidity of housing wealth, enabling homeowners to borrow cheaply against appreciating home values. Roughly 85% of college attendees come from homeowning families, and for most households the home is the dominant financial asset. With college costs rising and federal financial aid largely excluding home equity from need calculations, fluctuations in home values during this period plausibly altered the resources and borrowing capacity available to families with college-age children, especially those of modest means.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: DID — treatment = households experiencing housing wealth increase, control = households without significant change; shock/instrument/cutoff = regional housing price fluctuations

key_variables.treatment: households experiencing an increase in housing wealth
key_variables.control: households without significant change in housing wealth

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: An increase in liquid housing wealth positively affects college enrollment rates.
